theory.q: State and prove that curl(grad phi) = 0.
points: The i component is phi_zy - phi_yz
Mixed partial derivatives are equal, so it is 0
The j and k components vanish in the same way
Hence curl(grad phi) = 0

theory.q: State and prove that div(curl A) = 0.
points: div(curl A) is a sum of six second derivatives of the components
They are mixed partial derivatives that cancel in pairs
So the divergence of a curl is zero

theory.q: State the identity for the curl of a curl.
points: curl(curl A) = grad(div A) - nabla squared A
The Laplacian of a vector acts on each component

theory.q: State the product rules for div(phi A) and curl(phi A).
points: div(phi A) = phi div A + A . grad phi
curl(phi A) = phi curl A + grad phi x A

theory.q: State Laplace's and Poisson's equations and where they arise in electrical engineering.
points: For static fields E = -grad V because curl E = 0
Gauss's law div D = rho_v with D = epsilon E gives nabla squared V = -rho_v/epsilon (Poisson)
Where there is no charge nabla squared V = 0 (Laplace)
They determine the potential from the charge and the boundary conditions

theory.q: Say which combinations of grad, div and curl are meaningful and give two that are not.
points: grad takes a scalar and gives a vector; div takes a vector and gives a scalar; curl takes a vector and gives a vector
Meaningful combinations include div(grad), curl(grad), div(curl), curl(curl) and grad(div)
Div or curl of a scalar is not meaningful, and neither is grad of a vector in this sense

lessons.title: Line integrals
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 65 to 77 (Examples 2.2 and 2.3, Exercises 2.1 and 2.2); independence of path and the arc-length form are added
lessons.one_line: A line integral adds up a quantity along a curve: for a force it is the work done, and for a conservative field it depends only on the two end points.
lessons.analogy: Pushing a trolley along a winding road, the work you do is the sum, along the road, of the push in the direction of travel times each small step. That sum is a line integral. If the force is the pull of gravity, only the height you gain matters, not the winding of the road, and that is what a conservative field means.
recall: What is the dot product of (4, 4t, 3t^2) with (32t^4, 4t^4, -4t^5)?
What is the derivative of 3u with respect to u?
exam: For a curve $C$ the ordinary integral along the $x$-axis is replaced by an integral along the curve: $\int_C f\,ds=\int_A^Bf(x,y,z)\,ds$ (slide 65). In practice you write the curve in terms of a parameter, put everything in terms of it, and integrate between the parameter values of the end points.

Scalar field $V$ (slides 66 to 69): $\displaystyle\int_CV\,d\mathbf r$ with $d\mathbf r=dx\,\mathbf i+dy\,\mathbf j+dz\,\mathbf k$. The result is a vector: integrate $V\,dx$, $V\,dy$ and $V\,dz$ separately. Method: (1) put $x,y,z$ in terms of the parameter in $V$; (2) form $d\mathbf r$ by differentiating; (3) find the parameter values at the end points (the slide does this by solving $3u=3$, $2u^2=2$, $u^3=1$ to get $u=1$); (4) integrate.

Example 2.2: $V=xy^2z$, $x=3u$, $y=2u^2$, $z=u^3$ gives $V=12u^8$ and $d\mathbf r=3\,du\,\mathbf i+4u\,du\,\mathbf j+3u^2du\,\mathbf k$, so $\int_C V\,d\mathbf r=4\mathbf i+\tfrac{24}{5}\mathbf j+\tfrac{36}{11}\mathbf k$. Exercise 2.1 has answer $\tfrac{384}{5}\mathbf i+144\mathbf j+\tfrac{768}{11}\mathbf k$ (recomputed here and correct).

Vector field $\mathbf F$ (slides 71 to 76): $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=F_xdx+F_ydy+F_zdz$ and $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_CF_xdx+\int_CF_ydy+\int_CF_zdz$. The result is a number: the work done by the force $\mathbf F$ along $C$. Example 2.3: the integral is $\tfrac{128}{5}+\tfrac{8}{3}-\tfrac32=\tfrac{803}{30}=26\tfrac{23}{30}$. Exercise 2.2 has answer $7\tfrac{61}{168}=\tfrac{1237}{168}$ (recomputed and correct).

Arc length and scalar integrals with respect to arc length (not in the deck): $ds=\left|\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}\right|dt$, so the length of $C$ is $\int_C ds$ and $\int_Cf\,ds=\int f\,\left|\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}\right|dt$. Not in your notes.

Reversing direction: $\displaystyle\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=-\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$. For a closed curve the integral is written $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ and is called the circulation. Not in your notes.

Independence of path: if $\mathbf F=\nabla\phi$ (equivalently $\nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0$ in a region with no holes; lesson 6.8) then $\displaystyle\int_A^B\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(B)-\phi(A)$ for every path, and $\oint\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=0$ for every closed path. This is why gravity and electrostatic fields do no net work round a closed loop. Not in your notes.

lessons.title: Double and triple integrals
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 78 to 81 (Exercises 2.3 to 2.6, which give the questions only); the method is not in the deck
lessons.one_line: A double integral adds up a function over an area and a triple integral over a volume, by doing one single integral at a time from the inside out.
lessons.analogy: To add up the rainfall over a field you can add it row by row, then add the rows. A double integral does exactly that: the inner integral adds along one row, the outer integral adds up the rows. The only skill is writing down where each row starts and stops.
recall: What is the integral of 4y - y cubed from 0 to 2?
How do you find where y = x squared meets y = x?
exam: Double integral: $\displaystyle\iint_Rf(x,y)\,dA=\int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f\,dy\,dx$. The inner limits may depend on the outer variable. The outer limits are constants. The area of $R$ is $\iint_R1\,dA$. Not in your notes.

Method: (1) sketch the region and find where the boundary curves meet; (2) choose an order, $dy\,dx$ or $dx\,dy$; (3) write the limits: the outer variable runs between constants, and for each value of it the inner variable runs from the lower to the upper boundary; (4) integrate the inner integral first, treating the outer variable as a constant, then the outer integral. Not in your notes.

Either order gives the same answer, but one may be much easier. The slide's Exercise 2.3 ($f=4-y^2$, region bounded by $x=0$, $y=x$, $y=2$) asks for both: $\int_0^2\int_0^y(4-y^2)\,dx\,dy=4$ and $\int_0^2\int_x^2(4-y^2)\,dy\,dx=4$.

Area between curves (Exercise 2.4): the curves $y=5-x^2$ and $y=x+3$ meet at $x=-2$ and $x=1$, and the area is $\int_{-2}^{1}\left[(5-x^2)-(x+3)\right]dx=\tfrac92$, which the slide writes as $4\tfrac12$.

Triple integral: $\displaystyle\iiint_Vf\,dV=\iiint f\,dz\,dy\,dx$, with the innermost limits for $z$ depending on $x$ and $y$, the middle limits for $y$ depending on $x$, and constant outer limits for $x$. Constant limits for all three give a box and the integral separates. Not in your notes.

Exercise 2.5 asks only for the integral in order $dz\,dy\,dx$ for the solid between $z=2$ and $z=16-x^2-y^2$. The surfaces meet at $x^2+y^2=14$, so $\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{14}}^{\sqrt{14}}\int_{-\sqrt{14-x^2}}^{\sqrt{14-x^2}}\int_{2}^{16-x^2-y^2}f\,dz\,dy\,dx$. Exercise 2.6 (solid bounded by $z=0$, $z=x$, $y^2=4-2x$) gives $\displaystyle\int_0^2\int_{-\sqrt{4-2x}}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}\int_0^{x}f\,dz\,dy\,dx$. The deck prints no answers for these two; the volumes are $98\pi$ and $\tfrac{64}{15}$ (with $f=1$). Not in your notes.
Round regions: change to polar coordinates ($dA=r\,dr\,d\theta$) or, for solids, cylindrical or spherical ones (lesson 6.9), as the deck does for Exercise 2.5. Not in your notes.

lessons.title: Volume integrals
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 82 to 93 and 63 to 64 (Examples 2.5 and 2.6, the cylinder example, Exercise 2.7); the numbering clash and the word ``cubic'' are corrected
lessons.one_line: A volume integral adds up a field over a solid region; for a vector field you integrate each component separately and the answer is a vector.
lessons.analogy: To find the total mass of an unevenly packed box you cut it into tiny cubes, multiply each cube's volume by the density there, and add. A volume integral is that sum. For a vector field the same is done for each of the three components.
recall: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius 3 and height 4?
What is the volume element dV in cylindrical coordinates?
exam: Scalar field (slide 82): $\displaystyle\iiint_VF\,dV=\iiint F\,dx\,dy\,dz$, a scalar (for example a total mass when $F$ is a density). Vector field (slide 85): $\displaystyle\iiint_V\mathbf F\,dV$, a vector: integrate each component over the region.

Example 2.5 (slides 83 and 84): $F=2x$ over the box $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le3$, $0\le z\le2$ gives $\int_0^2\int_0^3\int_0^12x\,dx\,dy\,dz=6$. The slide calls the box a ``cubic'' and says the function is ``defeated'' in it; the words are cuboid and defined.

Example 2.6 (slides 86 to 89): $\mathbf F=2z\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf k$ over the tetrahedron bounded by $x=0$, $y=0$, $z=0$ and $2x+y+z=2$. The plane meets the axes at $(1,0,0)$, $(0,2,0)$ and $(0,0,2)$, so $x$ runs from $0$ to $1$, $y$ from $0$ to $2(1-x)$ and $z$ from $0$ to $2(1-x)-y$. The result is $\tfrac23\mathbf i+\tfrac13\mathbf k$.

Round solids: use cylindrical coordinates (slides 63 to 64 and 90 to 92): $x=\rho\cos\phi$, $y=\rho\sin\phi$, $dV=\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,dz$. For $\mathbf F=2\mathbf i+2z\,\mathbf j+y\,\mathbf k$ over $x^2+y^2\le9$, $0\le z\le4$, the result is $72\pi\,\mathbf i+144\pi\,\mathbf j$. The $\mathbf k$ component is zero because $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\phi\,d\phi=0$.

Numbering clash in the deck: this cylinder example is ``Example 2.1'' on slide 63 and ``Example 2.6'' on slide 90, the same label as the tetrahedron example. Treat them as two different examples. The example numbering in the deck skips and repeats in several places, but none of the answers is affected.

Exercise 2.7 (slide 93): $\mathbf F=3\mathbf i+z\,\mathbf j+2y\,\mathbf k$ over $x^2+y^2\le4$, $0\le z\le3$ gives $18\pi(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j)=36\pi\,\mathbf i+18\pi\,\mathbf j$ (recomputed and correct).
Symmetry shortcut: if the region is symmetric about a plane and the integrand is odd in the coordinate perpendicular to it, the integral is zero. Not in your notes.

lessons.title: Surface integrals
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 94 to 109 (Examples 2.7 and 2.8, Exercises 2.8 and 2.9); the orientation rule and the projection method are added
lessons.one_line: A surface integral adds up a field over a curved surface; for a vector field it measures how much of the field flows through the surface.
lessons.analogy: Hold a net in a river. The flux is the amount of water passing through the net each second. It depends on how fast the water moves, the area of the net, and how squarely the net faces the flow. If you tilt the net edge-on, nothing passes through.
recall: What is the unit normal to the surface x squared + y squared = 4?
What is dS on the wall of a cylinder in cylindrical coordinates?
exam: Scalar field (slide 94): $\displaystyle\int_SV\,d\mathbf S=\int_SV\,\hat{\mathbf n}\,dS$, a vector. Vector field (slide 102): $\displaystyle\int_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=\int_S\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dS$, a number called the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$. For a surface $\phi(x,y,z)=c$ the unit normal is $\hat{\mathbf n}=\dfrac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|}$ (lesson 6.6; the slides write $S$ for the function and for the surface, which is confusing, so the function is called $\phi$ here).

Orientation rule (not stated in the deck): a surface has two sides and the answer changes sign if the normal is reversed, so you must choose. For a closed surface the normal points outward. For an open surface the normal and the direction of its boundary go together by the right-hand rule: with your right thumb along $\hat{\mathbf n}$ the fingers curl in the direction in which the boundary is traversed, so the boundary runs counter-clockwise as seen from the tip of the normal (this is the rule used for Stokes' theorem). Not in your notes.

Method: (1) find $\hat{\mathbf n}$ from the gradient; (2) put the integrand in terms of the coordinates of the surface; (3) write $dS$ and the limits. For a cylinder wall of radius $a$: $x=a\cos\phi$, $y=a\sin\phi$, $dS=a\,d\phi\,dz$. For a sphere of radius $a$: $dS=a^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$. For a flat face, $dS$ is the area element of the plane ($dx\,dy$, $dy\,dz$ or $dx\,dz$) and $\hat{\mathbf n}$ is $\pm$ a unit vector.

Example 2.7 (slides 95 to 100): $V=xyz$ on $x^2+y^2=4$, $0\le z\le3$, first octant: $\nabla(x^2+y^2)=2x\mathbf i+2y\mathbf j$ has length $4$, so $\hat{\mathbf n}=\tfrac12(x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j)$, $\rho=2$, $dS=2\,d\phi\,dz$ with $0\le\phi\le\tfrac\pi2$, and the result is $12(\mathbf i+\mathbf j)$. Exercise 2.8 ($V=xyz^2$ on $x^2+y^2=9$, $0\le z\le2$): $24(\mathbf i+\mathbf j)$, recomputed and correct.

Example 2.8 (slides 103 to 108): $\mathbf F=y\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$ over the part of $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ in the first octant. $\hat{\mathbf n}=\tfrac13(x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+z\mathbf k)$, so $\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\tfrac13(xy+2y+z)$, and with $dS=9\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ the flux is $9\left(1+\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$. Exercise 2.9 ($\mathbf F=x\mathbf i+2z\mathbf j+y\mathbf k$ on the sphere of radius 2 in the first octant) has answer $8\left(\tfrac\pi6+1\right)$. The slide says ``a surface of the region'' but the answer matches the spherical part only, as in Example 2.8; the three flat faces are not included.

Projection method for a surface given by a function (not in the deck): if the surface is $\phi(x,y,z)=c$ and its shadow in the $xy$-plane is $R$, then $\displaystyle\int_S\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dS=\iint_R\frac{\mathbf F\cdot\nabla\phi}{\left|\partial\phi/\partial z\right|}\,dx\,dy$. For $\mathbf F=(x,y,z)$ on the plane $x+y+z=1$ this gives $\iint1\,dx\,dy=\tfrac12$ over the triangle. Not in your notes.

lessons.title: Green's theorem
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 110 to 118 (Example 2.9); the area formula and orientation are added
lessons.one_line: Green's theorem says the circulation of a field round a closed curve in a plane equals the total of its local swirl over the area inside.
lessons.analogy: Imagine a lake dotted with tiny whirlpools. Add up all the whirlpools inside the lake, and you get the same total as walking round the shore and adding up how much the current helps or hinders you. One sum is over the area, the other is along the boundary, and Green's theorem says they are equal.
recall: What is the area of a circle of radius 2?
What is the polar form of dx dy?
exam: Green's theorem (slide 110): if $C$ is a closed curve in the $xy$-plane, traversed counter-clockwise, enclosing a region $S$, and $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ are smooth, then $\displaystyle\iint_S\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy=\oint_C(P\,dx+Q\,dy)$.

It is Stokes' theorem (lesson 7.7) for a flat surface in the $xy$-plane, since $\mathbf F=P\mathbf i+Q\mathbf j$ has $(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\mathbf k=\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}$. Not in your notes.

The curve must be closed and traversed counter-clockwise, so that the region lies on the left; clockwise reverses the sign. The functions must have continuous first partial derivatives in the region. Not in your notes.
Example 2.9 (slides 111 to 118): $P=x^2+y^2$, $Q=x+2y$ on the quarter-disc bounded by $y=0$, $x=0$ and $x^2+y^2=4$ ($x,y\ge0$). The word ``prove'' here means verify both sides by calculation.

Line integral side: $C_1$ ($y=0$, $0\le x\le2$): $\int_0^2x^2dx=\tfrac83$. $C_2$ (the arc, $x=2\cos\theta$, $y=2\sin\theta$): $\pi-4$. $C_3$ ($x=0$, $y$ from $2$ to $0$): $\int_2^02y\,dy=-4$. Total: $\tfrac83+\pi-4-4=\pi-\tfrac{16}{3}$.

Area integral side: $\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}=1-2y$, and in polar coordinates $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^2(1-2r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta=\pi-\tfrac{16}{3}$. The two sides agree.

Area by Green's theorem: choosing $P=-\tfrac y2$, $Q=\tfrac x2$ gives $\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}=1$, so $A=\tfrac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. For a circle of radius $a$ this gives $\pi a^2$. Not in your notes.

lessons.title: The divergence (Gauss) theorem
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 119 to 131 (Example 2.10); applications and checks are added
lessons.one_line: The divergence theorem says that the total flux out of a closed surface equals the total divergence inside it, so a surface calculation can be replaced by a volume one.
lessons.analogy: Count the water pouring out of a bath through its whole surface and you get the same total as adding up how fast every tap and drain inside it is creating or removing water. The theorem says the net outflow through the boundary equals the sum of all the sources inside.
recall: What is the divergence of x i + 2j + z squared k?
What is the volume element in cylindrical coordinates?
exam: Divergence theorem (slide 119): for a closed surface $S$ enclosing a volume $V$ in a smooth vector field $\mathbf F$, $\displaystyle\iiint_V\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV=\oiint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=\oint_S\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dS$, with the normal pointing outward (the slide leaves out ``outward'').
Meaning: the divergence is the source strength per unit volume (lesson 6.7), so adding it over the whole region gives the total outflow through the boundary. Not in your notes.

Example 2.10 (slides 120 to 131): $\mathbf F=x\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+z^2\mathbf k$ in the region bounded by $z=0$, $z=4$, $x=0$, $y=0$ and $x^2+y^2=4$ (first octant). The word ``prove'' means verify that both sides agree.
Volume side: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1+2z$, and in cylindrical coordinates $\displaystyle\int_0^4\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^2(1+2z)\,\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,dz=20\pi$.

Surface side: five faces. $S_1$ ($z=0$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf k$): $\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=-z^2=0$, flux $0$. $S_2$ ($z=4$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=\mathbf k$): $\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=16$ over a quarter-disc of area $\pi$, flux $16\pi$. $S_3$ ($y=0$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf j$): $-2$ over a $2\times4$ rectangle, flux $-16$. $S_4$ ($x=0$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf i$): $-x=0$, flux $0$. $S_5$ ($x^2+y^2=4$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=\tfrac12(x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j)$, $dS=2\,d\phi\,dz$): flux $16+4\pi$.
Total: $0+16\pi-16+0+16+4\pi=20\pi$, equal to the volume side. Notice that the pieces $-16$ and $+16$ cancel, which is why the theorem is easier to use than the five-face calculation.

Checks and uses (not in the deck): the position field $\mathbf r$ has $
abla\cdot\mathbf r=3$, so its flux out of any closed surface is $3	imes$ the enclosed volume (for a sphere of radius $a$, $4\pi a^3$); a solenoidal field ($
abla\cdot\mathbf F=0$) has zero flux out of every closed surface. In electromagnetics, applying the theorem to $
abla\cdot\mathbf D=ho_v$ gives Gauss's law: the flux of $\mathbf D$ out of a closed surface equals the enclosed charge. Not in your notes.

lessons.title: Stokes' theorem
lessons.slides: Dr Jack's deck, slides 132 to 150 (Example 2.12; the deck has no Example 2.11, the numbering jumps from 2.10); the flat-surface check and the orientation rule are added
lessons.one_line: Stokes' theorem says the circulation of a field round the edge of a surface equals the total swirl of the field passing through the surface.
lessons.analogy: Take a net with a rim. The total of all the little whirlpools caught in the net equals the push you get from the current by walking once round the rim. It does not matter whether the net is flat or bulges like a bag, as long as it has the same rim.
recall: What is the curl of z i + x y j + x z k?
Which way round does the boundary go for a normal pointing upwards?
exam: Stokes' theorem (slide 132): if $\mathbf F$ is a smooth vector field on an open surface $S$ whose boundary is the closed curve $C$, then $\displaystyle\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$.

Orientation (not stated in the deck, and essential): the normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ of $S$ and the direction of $C$ go together by the right-hand rule. With the thumb along $\hat{\mathbf n}$ the fingers curl in the direction of $C$, so $C$ is traversed counter-clockwise as seen from the tip of $\hat{\mathbf n}$. Reversing either one changes the sign of its side. Not in your notes.
The surface $S$ is open (it has an edge), unlike the closed surface of the divergence theorem. Green's theorem (lesson 7.5) is the special case of a flat surface in the $xy$-plane. Not in your notes.

Example 2.12 (slides 133 to 150): $\mathbf F=z\mathbf i+xy\mathbf j+xz\mathbf k$. The surface $S$ is made of $S_1$, the curved wall of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=9$ for $0\le z\le4$, $y\ge0$; $S_2$, the half-disc at $z=4$; and $S_3$, the plane $y=0$ (a $6\times4$ rectangle). Its boundary $C$ lies in $z=0$: $C_1$ is the semicircle of radius 3 and $C_2$ is the straight line from $(-3,0,0)$ to $(3,0,0)$.

Surface side: $\nabla\times\mathbf F=(1-z)\mathbf j+y\,\mathbf k$. $S_1$ ($\hat{\mathbf n}=\tfrac13(x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j)$, $dS=3\,d\phi\,dz$): $(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\tfrac y3(1-z)$ gives $-24$. $S_2$ ($\hat{\mathbf n}=\mathbf k$): $\iint y\,dA=18$. $S_3$ ($\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf j$): $\iint(z-1)\,dz\,dx=24$. Total $-24+18+24=18$.

Line side: on $C_1$, $\mathbf F=9\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j$ and $d\mathbf r=(-3\sin\theta\,\mathbf i+3\cos\theta\,\mathbf j)\,d\theta$, so $\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_0^\pi27\sin\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=18$. On $C_2$, $\mathbf F=\mathbf 0$, so the integral is $0$. Total $18$, equal to the surface side.

Surface independence (not in the deck): only the boundary matters. The flat half-disc at $z=0$ with normal $\mathbf k$ has the same boundary, and $\iint y\,dA=18$ over it, which gives the same answer. So the curved part and the plane together contribute exactly what the flat surface does: the choice of surface is free. For $\mathbf F=-y\mathbf i+x\mathbf j$, a flat disc and a hemisphere of radius 2 both give $8\pi$. Not in your notes.

examples.title: Your slide 135: Example 2.12, the curl
examples.problem: $\mathbf F=z\,\mathbf i+xy\,\mathbf j+xz\,\mathbf k$. Find $\nabla\times\mathbf F$.

steps.m: \nabla\times\mathbf F=\left(\frac{\partial(xz)}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial z}\right)\mathbf i+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial(xz)}{\partial x}\right)\mathbf j+\left(\frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)\mathbf k

examples.title: Your slides 136 to 145: the surface side
examples.problem: Find $\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S$ over $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$.

steps.do: S1, the curved wall: n = (x i + y j)/3, rho = 3, dS = 3 d phi dz.
S2, the top half-disc: n = k.

examples.title: Your slides 146 to 150: the line side, and a flat surface
examples.problem: Find $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ round the boundary, and check with the flat half-disc at $z=0$.

steps.do: C1: x = 3 cos t, y = 3 sin t, z = 0, t from 0 to pi.
steps.m: \mathbf F=(0,\ 9\sin t\cos t,\ 0),\quad d\mathbf r=(-3\sin t,\ 3\cos t,\ 0)dt\Rightarrow\int_0^\pi27\sin t\cos^2t\,dt=18

steps.do: Check with the flat half-disc in z = 0, normal k.

steps.why: Stokes' theorem depends only on the boundary: any surface with the same edge gives the same answer.

examples.answer: $18$ both ways, and $18$ by the flat surface.

practice.q: Example 2.12. $\mathbf F=z\,\mathbf i+xy\,\mathbf j+xz\,\mathbf k$. Find $\nabla\times\mathbf F$ at $(1,2,3)$. Give $(x,y,z)$.
practice.hint: curl F = (1 - z) j + y k.

practice.q: For the curved wall $S_1$ ($x^2+y^2=9$, $0\le z\le4$, $y\ge0$) find $\iint(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S$. Give a number.
practice.hint: n = (cos phi, sin phi, 0), curl F . n = (1 - z) sin phi and dS = 3 d phi dz.

practice.q: For the top half-disc $S_2$ ($z=4$, $r\le3$, $y\ge0$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=\mathbf k$) find $\iint(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S$. Give a number.
practice.hint: curl F . k = y = r sin(theta).

practice.q: For the plane face $S_3$ ($y=0$, $\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf j$, $-3\le x\le3$, $0\le z\le4$) find $\iint(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S$. Give a number.
practice.hint: curl F . (-j) = z - 1.

practice.q: Add the three surface integrals $-24$, $18$ and $24$. This should equal $\oint\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ round the boundary. Give the total.
practice.hint: Add them.

practice.q: The boundary piece $C_1$ is the semicircle $x=3\cos\theta$, $y=3\sin\theta$, $z=0$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$. Find $\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$. Give a number.
practice.hint: On C1, F = (0, 9 sin(theta) cos(theta), 0) and dr = (-3 sin(theta), 3 cos(theta), 0) d theta.

practice.q: Use Stokes' theorem to find $\oint\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ for $\mathbf F=-y\,\mathbf i+x\,\mathbf j$ round the circle of radius 2 in the $xy$-plane, counter-clockwise. Give a decimal.
practice.hint: curl F = 2k, and the flat disc has area 4 pi.

practice.q: Use the hemisphere $z\ge0$ of radius 2 (outward normal) instead of the flat disc for the same $\mathbf F=-y\,\mathbf i+x\,\mathbf j$. Find $\iint(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S$. Give a decimal.
practice.hint: curl F . n = 2 cos(theta) and dS = 4 sin(theta) d theta d phi.

flashcards.back: $\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$.
Right-hand rule: counter-clockwise boundary as seen from the tip of the normal (not in your notes).
Any surface with the same boundary gives the same answer (not in your notes).
Green's theorem is Stokes' theorem for a flat surface in the xy-plane.

theory.q: State Stokes' theorem and the orientation rule.
points: The surface integral of curl F over an open surface S equals the line integral of F round its boundary C
The boundary direction and the normal are linked by the right-hand rule
C is counter-clockwise as seen from the tip of the normal
Reversing the normal reverses the direction of C

theory.q: Describe the surface and boundary used in Example 2.12.
points: S1 is the curved wall of the half-cylinder x squared + y squared = 9 for 0 <= z <= 4
S2 is the half-disc at z = 4 and S3 is the plane y = 0
The boundary is the semicircle C1 and the straight line C2 in the plane z = 0

theory.q: Find the curl of F = z i + xy j + xz k.
points: Expand the determinant
curl F = (1 - z) j + y k

theory.q: Evaluate the surface integral of curl F over S1, S2 and S3 in Example 2.12.
points: S1 gives -24
S2 gives 18
S3 gives 24
The total is -24 + 18 + 24, which is 18

theory.q: Evaluate the line integral of F round the boundary in Example 2.12 and compare.
points: On C1 the integral of 27 sin t cos squared t from 0 to pi is 18
On C2, F is zero so the integral is 0
The total is 18
This equals the surface side, so the theorem is verified

theory.q: Explain why a flat surface with the same boundary gives the same answer in Example 2.12.
points: Stokes' theorem depends only on the boundary curve
The flat half-disc at z = 0 has the same boundary
Its integral of y over the half-disc is 18

theory.q: Use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of F = -y i + x j round a circle of radius 2.
points: curl F = 2k
The flat disc has area 4 pi
The circulation is 2 times 4 pi = 8 pi

matrix.plain: A grid of numbers in rows and columns.
matrix.exam: A rectangular array of numbers (entries) arranged in rows and columns.

order.plain: How many rows by how many columns.
order.exam: A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m by n.

entry.exam: The element a_ij in row i and column j.

square-matrix.plain: A grid with as many rows as columns.

identity-matrix.plain: The matrix version of the number 1.
identity-matrix.exam: Square matrix with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere; AI = IA = A.

zero-matrix.exam: A matrix in which every entry is 0.

transpose.plain: Flip the grid so rows become columns.
transpose.exam: A transpose is obtained by interchanging rows and columns; an m by n matrix becomes n by m.

scalar.plain: An ordinary number, not a grid.
scalar.exam: A single number used to multiply every entry of a matrix.

stochastic-matrix.plain: A grid of probabilities where each row adds up to 1.
stochastic-matrix.exam: A matrix with non-negative entries whose rows each sum to 1 (name is standard, not in the notes).

row-column.plain: Rows go across; columns go down.
row-column.exam: Horizontal and vertical lines of entries in a matrix.

commutative.exam: An operation is commutative if the order of the operands does not change the result. Matrix multiplication is not.

determinant.plain: A single number worked out from a square grid.
determinant.exam: A scalar associated with a square matrix; for 2 by 2, a11 a22 - a12 a21.

minor.plain: What is left of a determinant when you cross out a row and a column.
minor.exam: The determinant obtained by deleting the row and column of an entry.

cofactor.plain: A minor with a plus or minus sign attached.
cofactor.exam: The minor of a_ij multiplied by (-1)^(i+j) (not in the notes).

singular-matrix.plain: A matrix that cannot be undone.
singular-matrix.exam: A square matrix with no inverse; its determinant is zero.

nonsingular-matrix.plain: A matrix that can be undone.
nonsingular-matrix.exam: A square matrix that has an inverse; its determinant is not zero.

cramers-rule.plain: Solve each unknown as one determinant divided by another.
cramers-rule.exam: x_k = D_k / D, where D_k replaces column k of D by the constants; needs D not zero.

linear-system.plain: A set of equations where the unknowns appear only to the first power.
linear-system.exam: Equations of the form a1 x1 + ... + an xn = b.

augmented-matrix.plain: The coefficient grid with the answers added as an extra column.
augmented-matrix.exam: [A | b], the coefficient matrix with the constants appended (not in the notes).

row-operation.plain: A move on the rows that keeps the solution the same.
row-operation.exam: Interchange two rows; multiply a row by a non-zero number; add a multiple of one row to another.

pivot.plain: The leading number in a row that you use to clear the numbers below it.
pivot.exam: The first non-zero entry in a row used in elimination.

row-echelon-form.plain: A staircase shape with zeros below the steps.
row-echelon-form.exam: A matrix with zeros below every leading entry.

back-substitution.plain: Solve the last equation first, then work upwards.
back-substitution.exam: Finding the unknowns from the bottom row of an echelon form upwards.

gaussian-elimination.plain: Tidy the equations into a staircase, then solve from the bottom.
gaussian-elimination.exam: Reduction of the augmented matrix to echelon form followed by back-substitution.

inverse-matrix.plain: The matrix that undoes another matrix.
inverse-matrix.exam: A^-1 with A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I.

gauss-jordan.plain: Row-reduce all the way to the identity to read off the inverse.
gauss-jordan.exam: Reducing [A | I] to [I | A^-1] using row operations (not in the notes).

homogeneous-system.plain: A set of equations whose answers are all zero.

trivial-solution.plain: The obvious solution where every unknown is zero.
trivial-solution.exam: x = 0, always a solution of a homogeneous system.

nontrivial-solution.plain: A solution where at least one unknown is not zero.
nontrivial-solution.exam: A solution x not equal to 0; exists for Ax = 0 only when det A = 0.

consistent.plain: A system that has at least one solution.
consistent.exam: A system with one or infinitely many solutions.

inconsistent.plain: A system whose equations contradict each other.

eigenvalue.plain: A number by which the matrix stretches a special direction.
eigenvalue.exam: A scalar lambda with Ax = lambda x for some x not zero; a root of det(A - lambda I) = 0.

eigenvector.plain: A direction that the matrix only stretches, never turns.
eigenvector.exam: A non-zero x with Ax = lambda x.

characteristic-equation.plain: The equation whose roots are the eigenvalues.

trace.plain: The total of the numbers down the main diagonal.
trace.exam: The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix; equals the sum of the eigenvalues (not in the notes).

periodic-function.plain: A function that repeats the same pattern again and again.
periodic-function.exam: f(x + T) = f(x) for all x; T is the period.

fourier-series.plain: A repeating wave written as a sum of sines and cosines.
fourier-series.exam: f(x) = a0/2 + sum of (a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx) for period 2 pi.

fourier-coefficient.plain: How much of one particular sine or cosine is in the wave.
fourier-coefficient.exam: The numbers a_n and b_n, found by integrating f against cos nx and sin nx over a period.

dirichlet-conditions.plain: The conditions that make a Fourier series work.
dirichlet-conditions.exam: Single-valued, finitely many jumps, maxima and minima in a period, and absolutely integrable.

even-function.plain: A function that looks the same when flipped left to right.
even-function.exam: f(-x) = f(x); its Fourier series has cosines only.

odd-function.plain: A function whose left half is the upside-down mirror of its right half.
odd-function.exam: f(-x) = -f(x); its Fourier series has sines only.

half-range-series.plain: A series for a function given only on half a period.
half-range-series.exam: A cosine series (even extension) or sine series (odd extension) on (0, L).

gamma-function.plain: The factorial extended to non-whole numbers.
gamma-function.exam: Gamma(n) = integral of x^(n-1) e^(-x) from 0 to infinity; Gamma(n + 1) = n Gamma(n).

beta-function.plain: An integral that shares a total between two powers, tied to the gamma function.
beta-function.exam: B(m, n) = integral of x^(m-1)(1-x)^(n-1) from 0 to 1 = Gamma(m)Gamma(n)/Gamma(m + n).

bessel-function.plain: A wave-like curve that fades away, arising in circular vibration problems.
bessel-function.exam: J_nu(x), a solution of x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - nu^2) y = 0.

fourier-integral.plain: The version of a Fourier series for a one-off, non-repeating function.
fourier-integral.exam: f(x) = (1/pi) integral of [A cos(wx) + B sin(wx)] dw from 0 to infinity.

fourier-transform.plain: A signal turned into a list of how much of each frequency it contains.
fourier-transform.exam: F(w) = integral of f(t) e^(-iwt) dt over all t.

laplace-transform.plain: A function of time turned into a function of s so calculus becomes algebra.
laplace-transform.exam: F(s) = integral of e^(-st) f(t) dt from 0 to infinity.

exponential-order.plain: A function that does not grow faster than an exponential.
exponential-order.exam: |f(t)| <= M e^(ct) for large t; guarantees the Laplace transform exists.

inverse-laplace-transform.plain: Getting the time function back from its s function.
inverse-laplace-transform.exam: f(t) = L^-1{F(s)}, found with partial fractions and the table.

partial-fractions.plain: Splitting a complicated fraction into simple ones.
partial-fractions.exam: Writing p(s)/q(s) as a sum of fractions with one factor of q in each denominator.

unit-step-function.plain: A switch that turns on at a chosen time.
unit-step-function.exam: u(t - a) = 0 for t < a and 1 for t > a.

auxiliary-equation.plain: The quadratic you get by guessing an exponential solution.
auxiliary-equation.exam: am^2 + bm + c = 0, from substituting y = e^(mx) into ay'' + by' + cy = 0.

general-solution.plain: All possible solutions, with arbitrary constants left in.
general-solution.exam: For a second-order equation, a solution with two arbitrary constants.

homogeneous-ode.plain: A differential equation with nothing on the right-hand side.
homogeneous-ode.exam: ay'' + by' + cy = 0, that is f(x) = 0.

superposition.plain: Adding solutions of a homogeneous equation gives another solution.
superposition.exam: If y1 and y2 solve the homogeneous equation, so does Ay1 + By2.

complementary-function.plain: The free behaviour of the system with no input.
complementary-function.exam: The general solution y_c of the homogeneous equation.

particular-integral.plain: One solution that responds to the input.
particular-integral.exam: Any one solution y_p of the full equation.

undetermined-coefficients.plain: Guess the shape of the answer and solve for the numbers in it.
undetermined-coefficients.exam: Trial form chosen from f(x), substituted, with coefficients equated.

initial-value-problem.plain: A differential equation plus the starting conditions.
initial-value-problem.exam: An equation with conditions such as y(0) and y'(0) fixing the constants.

cauchy-euler-equation.plain: An equation where each derivative is multiplied by the matching power of x.
cauchy-euler-equation.exam: x^2 y'' + a x y' + b y = 0, solved by y = x^m.

reduction-of-order.plain: Using one known solution to find a second.
reduction-of-order.exam: y2 = y1 times the integral of e^(-integral of P) / y1^2.

wronskian.plain: A number that tells whether two solutions are truly different.

variation-of-parameters.plain: A method that finds the particular integral for almost any input.
variation-of-parameters.exam: y_p = -y1 integral of y2 f / W + y2 integral of y1 f / W.

random-variable.plain: A number that depends on the outcome of an experiment.
random-variable.exam: A function giving a number to each outcome of a random experiment.

discrete-random-variable.plain: A variable that takes separate values, usually counts.
discrete-random-variable.exam: A random variable with a countable set of values, such as the number of heads.

continuous-random-variable.plain: A variable that can take any value in a range.
continuous-random-variable.exam: A random variable that can take any value in an interval, such as height.

probability-distribution.plain: A list of all outcomes and how likely each is.
probability-distribution.exam: The probabilities of all possible outcomes; they add to 1.

probability-mass-function.plain: The chance of each separate value of a discrete variable.
probability-mass-function.exam: p(x) = P(X = x), with the p(x) adding to 1.

probability-density-function.plain: A curve whose area gives probability.
probability-density-function.exam: f(x) >= 0 with total area 1; P(a <= X <= b) is the integral of f from a to b.

cumulative-distribution-function.plain: The probability of being at or below a value.
cumulative-distribution-function.exam: F(x) = P(X <= x); it rises from 0 to 1.

expected-value.exam: E[X] = sum of x p(x), or the integral of x f(x).

variance.plain: How spread out the values are.
variance.exam: E[X squared] minus the square of the mean; the standard deviation is its square root.

moment.plain: An average of a power of the variable.
moment.exam: The r-th moment about the origin is E[X^r].

moment-generating-function.plain: A formula that produces all the moments.
moment-generating-function.exam: M(t) = E[e^(tX)]; the r-th derivative at 0 is E[X^r].

binomial-distribution.plain: Counts successes in a fixed number of independent tries.
binomial-distribution.exam: P(X = x) = nCx p^x q^(n-x); mean np, variance npq.

poisson-distribution.plain: Counts rare events in an interval when you know the average.
poisson-distribution.exam: P(X = x) = e^(-lambda) lambda^x / x!; mean and variance lambda.

normal-distribution.exam: A symmetric continuous distribution with mean mu and standard deviation sigma.

standard-normal.plain: The bell curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
standard-normal.exam: Z = (X - mu)/sigma, with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

z-score.plain: How many standard deviations a value is from the mean.

scatter-plot.plain: A graph with one dot per pair of values.
scatter-plot.exam: A plot of (x, y) pairs used to see whether a linear relationship exists.

correlation-coefficient.plain: A number from -1 to 1 for how close to a straight line the data are.
correlation-coefficient.exam: Pearson's r, using the sums of x, y, xy, x squared and y squared.

coefficient-of-determination.plain: The share of the variation explained by the line.

spearman-rank-correlation.plain: Correlation of the rankings instead of the values.
spearman-rank-correlation.exam: rho = 1 - 6 sum d^2 / (n(n^2 - 1)) (not in the notes).

regression-line.plain: The best-fitting straight line, used to predict.
regression-line.exam: y = a + bx with b the slope and a = ybar - b xbar.

least-squares.plain: Choosing the line that makes the squared misses smallest.
least-squares.exam: Minimising the sum of the squares of the vertical deviations.

residual.plain: The vertical gap between a point and the line.

extrapolation.plain: Predicting outside the range of the data.
extrapolation.exam: Using the line beyond the observed x values; unreliable.

diagonalisation.plain: Rewriting a matrix as a list of stretch factors by changing to its eigenvector directions.
diagonalisation.exam: P^-1 A P = D, where the columns of P are eigenvectors and D holds the eigenvalues (not in the notes).

diagonal-matrix.plain: A grid with numbers only on the main diagonal.
diagonal-matrix.exam: A square matrix whose entries are zero off the main diagonal.

modal-matrix.plain: The matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors.
modal-matrix.exam: The matrix P of eigenvectors used in P^-1 A P = D.

lu-decomposition.plain: Splitting a matrix into a lower and an upper triangular matrix.
lu-decomposition.exam: A = LU with L lower triangular and U upper triangular (not in the notes).

lower-triangular.plain: A grid with zeros above the diagonal.
lower-triangular.exam: A square matrix with all entries above the main diagonal equal to zero.

upper-triangular.plain: A grid with zeros below the diagonal.
upper-triangular.exam: A square matrix with all entries below the main diagonal equal to zero.

forward-substitution.plain: Solving a lower triangular system from the first row down.
forward-substitution.exam: Solving Ly = b starting with y_1.

scalar-quantity.plain: A quantity with size only, such as a mass or a distance.
scalar-quantity.exam: A quantity with magnitude but no direction.

vector.plain: A quantity with both size and direction, such as a velocity.
vector.exam: A directed quantity written in components, x i + y j + z k.

unit-vector.plain: An arrow of length 1 used only to show a direction.
unit-vector.exam: A vector of magnitude 1; the unit vector of a is a / abs(a).

position-vector.plain: The arrow from the origin to a point.
position-vector.exam: OP = x i + y j + z k for the point (x, y, z).

direction-cosines.plain: The cosines of the angles a vector makes with the three axes.
direction-cosines.exam: The components of the unit vector; their squares add to 1 (not in the notes).

dot-product.plain: A number measuring how much two vectors point the same way.
dot-product.exam: a.b = a1 b1 + a2 b2 + a3 b3 = abs(a) abs(b) cos theta.

cross-product.plain: A vector perpendicular to two vectors whose length is the area they span.
cross-product.exam: a x b, the determinant with i, j, k; magnitude abs(a) abs(b) sin theta.

scalar-projection.plain: The length of the shadow of one vector along another.

scalar-triple-product.plain: A number whose size is the volume of the box on three vectors.
scalar-triple-product.exam: a.(b x c), the determinant of the three rows.

velocity.plain: How fast and in which direction a position is changing.
velocity.exam: The derivative of the position vector, dr/dt.

acceleration.plain: How fast the velocity is changing.
acceleration.exam: The second derivative of the position vector, d2r/dt2.

partial-derivative.plain: The rate of change with respect to one variable, the others held fixed.
partial-derivative.exam: The derivative with respect to one variable treating the others as constants.

vector-integral.plain: The integral of each component of a vector function.
vector-integral.exam: The integral of a vector function, taken component by component; the result is a vector.

del-operator.plain: A vector of three partial derivatives that acts on fields.
del-operator.exam: nabla = d/dx i + d/dy j + d/dz k, the vector differential operator.

gradient.plain: The vector pointing uphill, whose length is the steepness.
gradient.exam: grad phi = (phi_x, phi_y, phi_z), a vector function made from a scalar.

scalar-field.plain: A number attached to every point of space.
scalar-field.exam: A scalar function of position phi(x, y, z).

vector-field.plain: An arrow attached to every point of space.
vector-field.exam: A vector function of position A(x, y, z).

directional-derivative.plain: How fast a field changes if you move in a chosen direction.
directional-derivative.exam: d phi/ds = a-hat . grad phi, with a-hat a unit vector.

unit-normal.plain: A length-1 arrow perpendicular to a surface.
unit-normal.exam: n-hat = grad phi / abs(grad phi) for the surface phi = constant.

level-surface.plain: A surface on which a field has the same value everywhere.
level-surface.exam: The surface phi(x, y, z) = constant; the gradient is normal to it.

divergence.plain: How much a field is spreading out from a point.
divergence.exam: div A = dax/dx + day/dy + daz/dz, a scalar function.

solenoidal-field.plain: A field with no sources or sinks.
solenoidal-field.exam: A vector field with divergence zero everywhere (the slide says “solenoid vector”).

curl.plain: How much a field swirls around a point.
curl.exam: curl A = del cross A, a vector function; zero for an irrotational field.

irrotational-field.exam: A vector field with curl zero everywhere.

conservative-field.plain: A field whose line integral does not depend on the path.
conservative-field.exam: A field that is the gradient of a scalar potential, F = grad phi (not in the notes).

scalar-potential.plain: A single function from which a conservative field is found.
scalar-potential.exam: A scalar phi with F = grad phi (in electrostatics E = -grad V).

cylindrical-coordinates.plain: Coordinates that give distance from an axis, an angle round it, and a height.
cylindrical-coordinates.exam: (rho, phi, z) with x = rho cos phi, y = rho sin phi, z = z.

spherical-coordinates.plain: Coordinates that give distance from the origin and two angles.
spherical-coordinates.exam: (r, theta, phi) with theta from the z-axis and phi the azimuth.

volume-element.plain: A tiny piece of volume used for integrating.
volume-element.exam: dV: rho d rho d phi dz (cylindrical) or r squared sin theta dr d theta d phi (spherical).

laplacian.plain: The divergence of the gradient: a measure of how a quantity differs from its surroundings.
laplacian.exam: nabla squared phi = phi_xx + phi_yy + phi_zz (not in the notes).

harmonic-function.plain: A function that satisfies Laplace's equation.
harmonic-function.exam: A function with nabla squared phi = 0 (not in the notes).

line-integral.plain: Adding up a quantity along a curve.
line-integral.exam: The integral of a function or of F . dr along a curve C; for a force it is the work done.

parametrisation.plain: Describing a curve or surface with one or two helper variables.
parametrisation.exam: Writing x, y, z as functions of a parameter, so that an integral can be done in that parameter.

work-done.plain: The push along the direction of travel, added up along the path.
work-done.exam: W = the line integral of F . dr along the path.

double-integral.plain: Adding up a function over an area by doing two single integrals.
double-integral.exam: The integral of f(x, y) over a region R, written with two integral signs.

triple-integral.plain: Adding up a function over a volume by doing three single integrals.
triple-integral.exam: The integral of f(x, y, z) over a solid, with dV = dx dy dz.

region-of-integration.plain: The area or solid that the integral covers.
region-of-integration.exam: The set of points over which a double or triple integral is taken; its boundary gives the limits.

volume-integral.plain: A total of a field over a solid; a vector for a vector field.
volume-integral.exam: The integral of F dV over a solid region V; for a vector field each component is integrated.

surface-integral.plain: Adding up a field over a curved surface.
surface-integral.exam: The integral of V n dS (scalar field, a vector) or F . n dS (vector field, a number).

flux.plain: How much of a field flows through a surface.
flux.exam: The surface integral of F . n dS.

surface-orientation.plain: Which side of the surface the normal points to.
surface-orientation.exam: The choice of unit normal: outward for a closed surface; for an open surface, linked to the boundary by the right-hand rule.

greens-theorem.plain: Swirl added over an area equals the circulation round its edge.
greens-theorem.exam: The double integral of (dQ/dx - dP/dy) over S equals the line integral of P dx + Q dy round the boundary C, counter-clockwise.

circulation.plain: How much a field flows round a closed loop.
circulation.exam: The line integral of F . dr round a closed curve.

closed-curve.plain: A loop that ends where it starts.
closed-curve.exam: A curve whose end point is its starting point, such as a circle.

divergence-theorem.plain: Everything created inside a region flows out through its surface.
divergence-theorem.exam: The volume integral of div F over V equals the flux of F out of the closed surface S bounding V (Gauss' theorem).

closed-surface.plain: A surface that completely encloses a volume, like a balloon.
closed-surface.exam: A surface with no boundary curve; its normal is taken outward.

stokes-theorem.plain: Swirl passing through a surface equals the circulation round its rim.
stokes-theorem.exam: The surface integral of curl F over S equals the line integral of F round the boundary C of S; the orientation follows the right-hand rule.

past.q: Past test Q4. Find $k$ so that $4x_1+3x_2-x_3=0$, $7x_1-x_2-3x_3=0$, $3x_1-4x_2+kx_3=0$ has a non-trivial solution.
past.hint: Set the determinant of the coefficients to zero.

past.q: Past test Q5. Write the 3 by 3 identity matrix. (The original asks you to describe it: ones on the main diagonal, zeros elsewhere.)
past.hint: Ones on the diagonal, zeros everywhere else.
solution: The identity matrix has 1 in every diagonal position and 0 elsewhere.

past.q: Past test Q8 (adapted so it can be answered here). The determinant of the coefficient matrix of a system is zero. Which is true? Enter 1 for 'there is exactly one solution' or 2 for 'there are infinitely many solutions or none'.
past.hint: A zero determinant means there is no unique solution.
solution: With D = 0 the system is singular.
So there are infinitely many solutions or no solution.

past.q: Past test Q10 (a). $A=\begin{bmatrix}6&0&4\\1&5&-3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&9\\8&0\\-4&7\end{bmatrix}$. Find $A\cdot B$. (The original layout can be read two ways; this is the reading used in lesson 1.1.)
past.hint: A is 2 by 3 and B is 3 by 2, so the product is 2 by 2.

past.q: Past test Q10 (b). With the same $A$ and $B$, find $B\cdot A$.
Past test Q12. Show that $\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.3\\0.4&0.6\end{bmatrix}$ is a stochastic matrix by finding the sum of each row. Enter the common row sum.
solution: Every row sums to 1, so the matrix is stochastic.

past.q: Past test Q1. Find the unit vector of $B+2C$ if $B=13\mathbf a_x-7\mathbf a_y+6\mathbf a_z$ and $C=10\mathbf a_x-4\mathbf a_y+8\mathbf a_z$. Give $(x,y,z)$ as decimals.
past.hint: B + 2C = (33, -15, 22); divide by its magnitude sqrt(1798).

past.q: Past test Q2 (a). The original reads “the component of Ay perpendicular to F if E = 3ay + 4az and F = 4ax - 10ay + 5az”; read here as the component of $E$ perpendicular to $F$ (the “Ay” looks like a slip for E). Give the perpendicular component vector $(x,y,z)$.
past.hint: E perp = E minus (E.F / abs(F) squared) F, with E.F = -10 and abs(F) squared = 141.

past.q: Past test Q2 (b). With the same $E$ and $F$, give the magnitude of the perpendicular component.
Past test Q3 (adapted: evaluated at $(1,2,3)$ so that it can be checked). Find the gradient of $U=x^2y+xyz$ at $(1,2,3)$. Give $(x,y,z)$.
past.hint: The general gradient is (2xy + yz) a_x + (x^2 + xz) a_y + xy a_z.

past.q: Past test Q6. Find the angle, in degrees, between $B=13\mathbf a_x-7\mathbf a_y+6\mathbf a_z$ and $C=10\mathbf a_x-4\mathbf a_y+8\mathbf a_z$. Give a decimal.
past.hint: B.C = 206, abs(B) squared = 254 and abs(C) squared = 180.

past.q: Past test Q11 (adapted: evaluated at $(1,2,3)$). Find the gradient of $xy+yz+x^2$ at $(1,2,3)$. Give $(x,y,z)$.
past.hint: The general gradient is (y + 2x) a_x + (x + z) a_y + y a_z.
